While Rome Burns, Nero Plays the Flute!! #The Crisis of Priorities in the ʿUlamāʾ Community and the Self-Satisfaction Derived from Trivial Disputes

One of Satan’s subtle strategies concerning the ʿulamāʾ is to make the more important and higher-priority responsibilities appear to them as risky, complicated, or contrary to their own positions and interests.

Yet their attention, intellect, and collective efforts are most urgently needed in addressing the fundamental problems of the dīn and society, confronting contemporary intellectual challenges, and playing an effective role in broader programmes of reform.

Instead of these important responsibilities, however, Satan makes relatively secondary, fragmented, and less significant issues appear exceedingly attractive and important. Consequently, the ʿulamāʾ become preoccupied with such matters, engage in mutual disputes and conflicts, and sometimes derive a sense of self-satisfaction from this very preoccupation and mutual bickering.

They may not even realise that, by avoiding more important responsibilities and immersing themselves in comparatively less significant matters, they are essentially making serious errors in setting their priorities.

In this connection, it is worth recalling a widely circulated historical anecdote.

It is said that during the decline of Muslim Andalusia, particularly around the final catastrophe of Granada, when Christian forces were capturing Muslim territories one after another and the very existence of Muslim rule was under threat, a section of the ʿulamāʾ and intellectuals remained engrossed in various secondary and theoretical disputes instead of addressing the greater crisis.

According to popular accounts, the subjects of their debates included:

- Whether the blood of fish is pure or impure, and whether a garment stained with it could be worn while performing Ṣalāh;

- Whether it is possible to see Allah Almighty in a dream and, if so, what the nature of such a vision might be;

- The structure of angels’ wings, or how many angels could stand on the head of a needle;

- Even whether marriage between jinn and human beings is permissible, and what the rules governing marriage and inheritance among jinn would be.

Some versions of the anecdote also describe lengthy arguments and mutual disputes over these matters.

Of course, reliable contemporary historical sources clearly documenting these specific disputes are not readily identifiable. Nevertheless, the underlying message of this popular anecdote is profoundly significant:

When a society and civilisation are facing an existential crisis, it is deeply alarming if their intellectual and religious leadership remains preoccupied with secondary and relatively insignificant matters instead of confronting the larger challenges.

In reality, this is not a call to abandon all differences of opinion or to put an end to scholarly discussions and juristic debates. There is a recognised and necessary space for the pursuit of knowledge, exchange of views, and *ikhtilāf* (scholarly disagreement).

The real question is how much importance a particular issue deserves and which responsibility should take priority at a given time.

The fact that an issue is worthy of scholarly discussion does not necessarily make it the most important issue under all circumstances. In particular, when a broader crisis confronts society and the Ummah, the hallmark of responsible leadership is the ability to determine priorities in light of actual needs and prevailing circumstances.

The widely circulated metaphor, *“While Rome was burning, Nero was playing the flute,”* symbolises precisely this kind of irresponsible indifference and misplaced self-satisfaction.

May our ʿulamāʾ community never fall victim to a situation in which the greater crises surrounding them remain beyond their field of vision, while debates over secondary and relatively less important matters become their principal preoccupation and the very measure of their sense of achievement.
